newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan to resume talks on April 9.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan to resume talks on April 9.

text.p: Pakistan said on Saturday it would resume peace talks with India next week despite a political crisis in New Delhi, and hoped the two neighbours could eventually resolve their disputes, including Kashmir.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan said he would meet his Indian counterpart, Inder Kumar Gujral, on April 9, two days before Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda faces a vote of confidence in parliament in New Delhi.

"We would like to resolve our disputes, and the core issue is naturally Kashmir," Khan told reporters after he arrived in the Indian capital to attend a two-day meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) starting on Monday.

Khan said he and Gujral would meet over breakfast on April 9 to carry forward discussions held last month between the two countries' foreign secretaries, the top-ranking civil servants in their foreign ministries.
"This will be our contact and it's to further progress on what our foreign secretaries of both sides discussed here in New Delhi for four days," Khan said.
The foreign secretaries ended four days of upbeat talks on March 31 and agreed to hold a subsequent round of negotiations in Islamabad.
But they did not set a date for their next meeting, partly because of political uncertainty in Delhi, where Deve Gowda's minority government faces the vote of confidence on April 11.

On Tuesday, Khan said his talks with Gujral might be put off because of the looming trust vote. Gujral said on the same day that it would be understandable if bilateral talks did not go ahead as planned.

But the two sides have since decided to go ahead with the negotiations in spite of the political uncertainty, which has appeared to wane as the possibility of a patch-up between Deve Gowda's ruling coalition and the rival Congress party emerges.

Asked if he was confident the two sides could narrow differences despite the political crisis in New Delhi, Khan said: "We've kept the 9th morning breakfast meeting as I've not met the honourable foreign minister before."

Khan said he believed there would be progress in Indo-Pakistani relations, and that the foreign secretaries would meet again in Islamabad to be followed by a meeting of the two nations prime ministers during a regional summit in May.
"We hope to continue the process of normalisation and to try and solve the problems we have and the disputes that we have," the visiting foreign minister said.
Khan's reference to Kashmir as the "core issue" reflects Pakistan's longstanding view that the foes must concentrate on settling their dispute over the Himalayan region before tackling other issues.

But New Delhi is prepared to reach agreements in other, unrelated areas before resolving their differences over Kashmir, the cause of two of the three wars which India and Pakistan have fought since independence from Britain in 1947.
India, which controls two thirds of Kashmir, accuses Pakistan of arming and training separatist guerrillas fighting New Delhi's rule in Jammu and Kashmir.
Pakistan, which rules over the remaining one third, says it provides the separatists only political and diplomatic support.

Earlier on Saturday, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan urged India and Pakistan to press ahead with bilateral talks, saying he was excited by the prospect of peace in the region. Annan, like Khan, was in India to attend the NAM meeting.
